010.md:
You didn't say what the email is about, so I've written the most common version of it: asking your boss for a couple of days off. I've used Thursday and Friday as the example.

Subject: Time off request: Thursday and Friday

Hi [Manager],

I'd like to ask for Thursday and Friday off. I'm raising it now so it can go into the schedule while there's still room to move things around.

Coverage for both days is already sorted: a colleague has agreed to take them and has confirmed that with me. Anything urgent on my side will be finished before I go, and I'll leave notes on the rest so nothing sits waiting on me.

Would you approve those two days?

Thanks,
[Your name]

That's 90 words with the subject line. If it's about something else (a raise, a deadline slipping, a complaint), tell me which one and I'll rebuild it to the same shape.
010.note: The success spec alone gets the form exactly right, under 120 words with the ask in the opening sentence and a yes-or-no close, but with no context it has to invent a plausible request and fill that form with a hypothetical colleague, a hypothetical Thursday and a manager it can only address as [Manager].

110.md:
Here's a draft you can send more or less as-is.

Subject: Time off request for next Thursday and Friday

Hi Renee,

My sister is getting married next weekend and I'll be away for it. I'd like to ask for next Thursday and Friday off, which is three weeks out, so hopefully it's early enough to build around.

Marcus already said he'd take my Thursday shift. Friday is the only one still open, and I'll keep asking around if that would help. I know things are busy, and I completely understand if not.

I haven't asked for a day off since I started, so this isn't something that'll become a habit.

Is that okay with you?

Thanks,

Add your name at the bottom. If Renee comes back worried about Friday, that's the moment to offer to find someone yourself, rather than putting it in this first message.
110.note: Context plus the spec produces a real email about Renee, the wedding, Marcus and the three weeks of notice, still inside the 120-word limit, but with the keyword lever off it writes on instinct rather than craft: the ask slides into the second sentence and the closing softener hands Renee a ready-made no.

011.md:
Since I don't know the actual request, I've put a stand-in scheduling request into the structure; the shape is what transfers. Keep the subject line specificity when you swap your own details in, because naming the decision rather than the topic is what survives inbox triage.

Subject: Approval needed: shift swap on the 18th

Hi [Manager's name],

I'd like to swap out of my shift on the 18th. Priya has agreed to take it and is already trained on everything that shift covers, so the desk is staffed either way.

Nothing else on the schedule moves. I'm picking up her Sunday morning in exchange, so the hours come out even on both sides, and I'll put the change on the shared calendar as soon as you confirm.

Does that swap work for you?

Thanks,

What's carrying it: the ask is front-loaded into the first sentence, BLUF style, so a partial read still lands it, and sentence two settles the coverage before she can raise it, which drops her response cost to a single word. No throat-clearing ahead of the ask, no qualifier or concession trailing behind it, no deference dressed up as manners. The closing question is a yes/no close rather than an open one, since open questions add decision latency. Reciprocity does the persuading, and the tone register stays level: direct, not demanding.
011.note: The keyword lever turns the spec's word limit into an actual rhetorical structure, ask first, constraint resolved second, one unhedged call to action, and then names its own moves, but with no context it is expert work spent on an invented shift swap for a manager it has never met.

111.md:
Subject: Next Thursday and Friday off, Thursday already covered

Hi Renee,

I'd like Thursday and Friday of next week off for my sister's wedding. Marcus has already agreed to take Thursday, so Friday is the only shift that still needs a name on it.

I'm bringing this to you three weeks out so it lands before the schedule goes up, and I'll keep asking around for Friday in the meantime. If someone says yes, I'll send you the name.

This is the first time I've asked for a day off since I started.

Can you approve both days?

Thanks,

Three notes on the build. The BLUF opening matters more than it looks: Renee reads this between two other things, so front-loading the ask and sequencing the rest behind it means the email survives a one-line read. The framing of Marcus's shift does the other half, "has already agreed" rather than a passive construction like "Thursday would be covered," which makes the coverage a solved problem instead of a favor. Favors spend social capital you'll want later.

The missing line is deliberate. Most drafts close with something like "I completely understand if not." It reads as deference, but that final concession writes her refusal for her and cuts the response cost of a no to zero. The first-time-asking line does that job better: pure salience.

One call to action, no hedging language, and a binary close she can answer in a word, which keeps her decision latency low, the tone register level, and leaves you a paper trail if the schedule shifts.
111.note: All three levers at once: the spec's 120 words, the context's Renee and Marcus and three-week notice, and the keyword lever's insistence on leading with the ask, so the coverage arrives as a settled fact in sentence two and the softener that would have handed Renee an exit is gone on purpose.
